A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AutoDAN-Turbo research. Their text, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

before.justification: v3 reports original jailbreak evaluations, strategy-transfer experiments, human-strategy injection experiments, and query-efficiency measurements.

after.justification: v4 retains those empirical results and adds query-budget scaling, prompt-diversity measurements, human-agreement evaluations, and a scoring ablation.

M1.justification: Appendix F introduces AutoDAN-Turbo-sorting, an alternative using categorical response comparisons and modified strategy retrieval. Section 3.3 also corrects the ineffective-strategy condition from a strategy count below two to the highest score below two. The principal framework remains unchanged; the new pseudocode largely documents existing stages.

E1.justification: Appendix F adds human-validation tasks involving 42 response-scoring cases and 20 strategy-summary cases, evaluated by five external raters. The existing jailbreak datasets and malicious-request coverage are retained; the diversity and query-budget experiments do not introduce additional jailbreak domains.

E2.justification: Table D adds AutoDAN-Turbo-sorting as a directly evaluated comparator. The comparator memberships in the retained benchmark and query-efficiency tables are unchanged. Appendix J's additional discussion of AutoDAN does not introduce a new baseline evaluation.

E3.justification: New protocols include six lifelong-learning query budgets from 4,000 to 50,000, diversity measurements using BLEU and embedding similarity, and multiple-choice human validation. Diversity sampling uses 20 requests with ten prompts each and a separate set of 100 requests. These substantially extend evaluation design while retaining the main benchmark training and testing schedule.

E4.justification: Appendices B, C, and F add query-budget sensitivity, within- and across-request prompt diversity, human validation of scorer and summarizer reliability, and numerical-scoring versus categorical-ranking ablation. These investigate several previously untested properties. The earlier transfer analyses largely remain, although the Llama-2-13B attacker dataset-transfer panel is removed.

E5.justification: Appendix F newly reports chance-corrected agreement estimates using Cohen's kappa against five human evaluators. Neither version reports attack-run confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. v4 does not specify how the five evaluators' judgments are aggregated into the reported kappa values.

E6.justification: Tables 1–5 retain identical numerical results. New Tables A–D report scaling, diversity, human agreement, and scoring-ablation outcomes; for example, Table D reports 38.8 ASR for the original method versus 34.4 for sorting on Llama-3-70B at 8,000 queries. v3 Figure 4(b)'s Llama-2-13B attacker transfer results disappear; the other three transfer plots retain their values.

T1.justification: Neither version develops theoretical guarantees or proofs, and the existing mathematical description of strategy construction is retained. The added algorithm outlines primarily restate the procedure, while Equation S1 supplies the standard Cohen's kappa formula for the new empirical evaluation.

C1.justification: The abstract and principal introduction and conclusion claims remain unchanged: autonomous strategy discovery, black-box operation, strategy transferability, compatibility with human-designed strategies, and superior reported attack performance. The added studies support these claims without redefining the central contribution.

C2.justification: v4 adds substantive interpretations connecting continual exploration to scaling, human agreement to attack effectiveness, and categorical scoring's weaker performance to insufficient retrieval discrimination. It also interprets the new diversity measurements. Section 4.2 removes the explicit assertion that Rainbow Teaming's fixed strategy set causes its lower ASR; the computational-resource limitation is retained under a separate heading.

D1.justification: v4 adds stage-by-stage pseudocode, explicitly identifies Llama-3 Instruct and Gemma-1.1 checkpoints, explains first-iteration prompting, and discloses exclusion of strategy examples when supplying existing categories to the summarizer. These improve documentation without establishing experimental reruns. Existing full prompts, hardware guidance, and code-access links remain.

R1.justification: v4 adds citations to Papineni et al. for BLEU and Smeeton for kappa. New Appendix J explicitly distinguishes AutoDAN-Turbo from AutoDAN by framework, initialization, and access assumptions, using the existing Table 2 comparison. The main related-work discussion is otherwise retained.

P1.justification: Most existing prose remains unchanged. v4 adds localized explanations and cross-references, reorganizes and expands the appendices, separates the limitations paragraph, adds acknowledgments, and changes the preprint header to the ICLR 2025 publication header. This is not an extensive rewrite of the existing narrative.

P2.justification: v4 adds four experimental tables and three algorithm displays. Figure 4 becomes a single Gemma attacker plot with surrounding text; the Llama-3-70B and Gemini panels move to Appendix Figure B, while the Llama-2-13B panel is removed. The original prompt table moves and becomes Table E, substantially reorganizing the supporting displays.

improvement.justification: The added component validation, scoring ablation, diversity measurements, and training-budget analysis improve support for previously underexamined properties, while pseudocode improves accessibility. The gain is limited by unspecified aggregation of human judgments, a scaling-summary inconsistency—five of six winners claimed versus six of seven in Table A—and removal of one transfer panel. The main benchmark evidence remains unchanged.
